# Silk Roads: goods, directions and route notes

The slider selects four broad historical snapshots: c. 1300 BCE, 150 CE,
900 CE and 1300 CE. The dates centre periods rather than claim that every
illustrated exchange occurred in one calendar year. These are representative
exchanges, not recovered shipment tracks or measures of volume. Goods changed hands at intermediate markets. The lanes
are separated in screen pixels for readability, not because caravans used
parallel roads. Story copy and the legend are in `history/<period>.md`.

## Commodities

- **Silk:** Chinese silk moved west through Central Asia toward the Mediterranean,
  and south toward India. [UNESCO's overview](https://www.unesco.org/en/silk-roads/about-silk-roads)
  describes its arrival in the Roman world and the changing land and sea networks.
  The later snapshots preserve alternative overland corridors; their visibility
  does not establish equal traffic or continuous use at every point in the period.
- **Gold and silver:** These are grouped as metals, including coins, bullion and
  objects; money is not a separate cargo category. The eastern overland flow is
  an illustrative chain of exchanges into Central Asia, not a documented single
  Roman shipment to Samarkand. The Indian Ocean branch has direct textual support
  in the [first-century Periplus, sections 49 and 56](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/periplus/periplus.html).
- **Glass, copper and tin:** The Periplus records western supplies of glass and
  these metals to Indian ports. They share a color here because the same broad
  maritime connection is shown, not because they were one product or always one
  cargo. Tin's inclusion reflects raw-material trade for manufacturing, including
  bronze; it does not imply that all tin originated in the city of Rome.
- **Horses:** A representative Fergana-to-China connection, joining the existing
  Kashgar and northern Tarim corridors. The [Fergana-Syrdarya nomination](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6568)
  discusses the region's horses and its Silk Roads exchanges. This selected
  itinerary does not exclude other passes, steppe sources, tribute or diplomacy.
- **Spices and cotton:** Indian ports supplied spices and textiles to western
  buyers, described by the Periplus. The regional network includes Barygaza and
  the Malabar connection around Muziris, with inland and coastal feeder routes.
  Goods could arrive from elsewhere before being re-exported.

## Regional networks and Constantinople

The regional links in `tour-trade-regions.mjs` replace the earlier single-terminal
treatment of China, India and Europe. They select a few major connecting corridors,
not every road, the maximal borders of empires, or an empire-wide goods inventory.
Connecting waypoints are editorial, not extracted GIS tracks. A commodity color
on an internal route represents collection or distribution; it does not establish
that every named city manufactured or mined every item in that category.

- **China:** Luoyang connects the eastern network to Chang’an. Jiangnan’s
  Hangzhou–Suzhou–Yangzhou region feeds the Sui–Tang canal corridors; a separate
  Yangtze/central-plains connection and the Sichuan–Qinling connection form inland
  branches. The north reaches Youzhou, and the south follows the broad
  Pearl–Lingqu–Xiang connection to the Yangtze. Sources:
  [Chang’an–Tianshan corridor](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1442/),
  [Grand Canal](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1443/),
  [Lingqu Canal](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5814), and
  [Chinese sericulture regions](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/sericulture-and-silk-craftsmanship-of-china-00197).
  These waterways developed in different eras; their inclusion does not mean
  that the complete illustrated network operated under the Han.
- **India:** Mathura, the Ganges plain and Tamralipti connect to Ujjain and
  Barygaza; the Deccan branches through Paithan, while the west coast reaches
  Muziris and crosses the Palghat gap toward the Tamil coast at Arikamedu.
  Sources: [Ujjain district history](https://ujjain.nic.in/en/history/),
  the Periplus, the Met’s [Gandhara study and trade maps](https://resources.metmuseum.org/resources/metpublications/pdf/The_Art_of_Gandhara_in_The_Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art.pdf), and
  [Kerala’s Muziris project](https://www.keralatourism.org/muziris/muziris-project/spice-route).
  Coast and river positions are approximate modern geographic anchors; southern
  ports and the Ganges valley were not always under the same ruler.
- **Roman Europe:** Iberia’s Mediterranean connection, the Rhône, Rhine/Moselle,
  Britain–Gaul connection and the Po valley link with Rome. Regional movement
  combines land, river and coastal travel. [Stanford’s ORBIS research](https://history.stanford.edu/publications/orbis-stanford-geospatial-network-model-roman-world)
  informs the choice of a connected multimodal network, but these simplified
  coordinates are not a downloaded ORBIS itinerary or a trade-volume model.
- **Byzantium / Constantinople:** The city joins the Anatolian corridor from
  Antioch, Aegean ports, and the Via Egnatia through Thessaloniki and Dyrrachium,
  then the Adriatic crossing and Via Appia toward Rome. An Alexandria–Levant
  connection brings the Indian Ocean trade into this eastern Mediterranean
  network. Sources: [UNESCO’s Culture of Trade](https://en.unesco.org/silkroad/sites/default/files/knowledge-bank-article/the%20culture%20of%20trade.pdf)
  and the [Greek Ministry of Culture’s Via Egnatia history](https://culturalegnatia.culture.gov.gr/en/the-via-egnatia-through-the-ages/).
  Constantinople’s prominence belongs especially to late antiquity and the
  Byzantine era. Silk later had other production centres, including Byzantium;
  the cream flow highlights the Chinese connection without claiming a permanent
  Chinese monopoly.

## Geography and chronology

The existing overland oasis and mountain-pass network follows the sources listed
in `tour-route-data.mjs`, including the [University of Washington route survey](https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/exhibit/trade/essay.html).
Its named places are geographic anchors. The Antiquity view substitutes
Ctesiphon for Baghdad and removes the Sui–Tang canal and Constantinople hub.
The medieval views replace the Roman western network and its maritime ports.

The added Rome–eastern Mediterranean and Rome–Alexandria legs represent sea
connections. Alexandria connects through the Nile valley and an overland desert
transfer to Berenike, then through the Red Sea and Indian Ocean to western India.
There is no modern Suez Canal shortcut. These are schematic corridors, not
navigation tracks or the only seasonal sailing itineraries.
The [Metropolitan Museum's Roman–Asian trade overview](https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/trade-between-the-romans-and-the-empires-of-asia)
documents the combination of Mediterranean shipping, caravan routes, Red Sea
ports and Nile transfers. Roman maritime legs are used in Antiquity. The medieval views instead use
Gulf ports, southern Chinese shipping and later Mediterranean connections.


## Four historical snapshots

### Bronze Age · c. 1300 BCE

This is a Mediterranean and western Asian exchange network before the late
Bronze Age collapse, not an early China-to-Rome Silk Road. Six color groups
separate tin, copper, gold, glass, timber and textiles/pottery. All joining
waypoints are editorial. They do not identify a merchant’s exact journey.

- [Williams et al., Antiquity (2025)](https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2025.41)
  supplies new chemical and isotopic evidence for southwest British tin in
  Mediterranean finds. This supports a source-to-market connection, not a
  recovered route across France. The map chooses one **hypothetical**
  Channel–continental–Mediterranean chain and marks its tin legs as uncertain.
  Other itineraries and sources are possible. The authors explicitly discuss
  contamination complicating the provenance of Uluburun tin; the map does not
  claim that all of that cargo came from Cornwall.
- The proposed **Central Asia / Afghan Hindu Kush → Iran → Mesopotamia →
  Ugarit → Cyprus → Crete** corridor adds an eastern possibility. Regional
  source anchors join near Bactria before continuing across Iran; they are not
  mapped mines, dated merchant stops or a claim that every leg operated together
  in precisely 1300 BCE. All five eastern tin legs retain the uncertain styling
  and the same illustrative frequency as western tin.
  [Berger et al. (2023), Central Asian bronze](https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2023.1224873)
  documents Bronze Age mining in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and discusses Afghan
  tin resources. Its direct link between Mushiston and regional bronze objects
  does **not** establish Mediterranean exports: the study finds no demonstrated
  distribution beyond 500 km. The companion
  [Uluburun provenance reassessment (2023)](https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2023.1211478)
  challenges the 2022 Central Asian attribution while leaving Afghan sources
  among the possibilities. The drawn westward chain is an editorial hypothesis,
  not a resolution of that debate or evidence of a dominant supplier.
- The excavators’ [Uluburun account](https://nauticalarch.org/projects/uluburun-late-bronze-age-shipwreck-excavation/)
  documents copper and tin cargo, glass, pottery and luxury materials. This is
  evidence for interconnected markets and mixed cargoes, not proof that our
  drawn lines reproduce the ship’s full itinerary. Cypriot copper supplies the
  regional copper branches; the coastal anchors represent ports and exchanges,
  not mine locations.
- [Cline’s research overview](https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/gw-professor-investigates-year-civilization-collapsed)
  treats the collapse as a combination of stresses. The story therefore links
  disrupted trade with warfare, drought and political upheaval without claiming
  that a tin shortage alone caused the collapse. It also avoids presenting the
  crisis as a simultaneous worldwide end of Bronze Age societies.

### Antiquity · c. 150 CE

Roman, Parthian, Kushan and Han connections draw on the
[Met’s Roman–Asian trade overview](https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/trade-between-the-romans-and-the-empires-of-asia)
and the Periplus cited above. Regional Roman roads return in this view; later
Baghdad, the Sui canal and the imperial Constantinople network do not. The
Bronze Age’s separate tin color is folded into the documented western
manufactured-goods/metals group here. These snapshots are selective, not
exhaustive inventories of commodities or all steppe communities.

### Early Middle Ages · c. 900 CE

This covers connections developing across the 9th–10th centuries, including
late Tang China (the dynasty ended in 907). Baghdad and Siraf connect the Gulf
with India; Guangzhou anchors southern Chinese shipping. Wars and the late
9th-century disruption of Guangzhou trade mean that the sea corridor should
not be read as uninterrupted annual service.

The Baltic–Volga and Dnieper branches include overland portages. The
[British Museum’s Silk Roads materials](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/2024-09/Silk_Roads_Exhibition_activity_cards_KS3.pdf)
describe Scandinavian access to eastern networks and the exchange of enslaved
people for Islamic silver. [Bolgar’s archaeological record](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/981/)
anchors the Volga network. The furs layer is explicitly furs only; slavery is
acknowledged in the text, not silently represented by the same commodity dots.
Silver lines combine several sources and intermediaries, including Samanid
Central Asia. They are schematic exchange chains, not a claim that Baghdad
mined all the silver or that one northern ethnicity controlled the entire route.

For Central Asian context, see
[Zarafshan–Karakum](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1675/) and the study of
[Islamic Iran’s trade connections](https://en.unesco.org/silkroad/sites/default/files/knowledge-bank-article/the_civilization_of_islamic_iran_cultural_hegemony_along_the_silk_road.pdf).
The Indian port changes use medieval Kollam, Gujarat and Tamil coast anchors,
not an unchanged Roman-era Muziris/Arikamedu network. See the University of
Kerala study of [Chinese coins and trade at Kollam](https://www.heritageuniversityofkerala.com/JournalPDF/Volume5/53.pdf).
Inland connections are simplified geographic corridors rather than proof of
unchanging river channels or each city’s relative importance.

### High Middle Ages · c. 1300 CE

The [Volga–Caspian corridor nomination](https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6569/)
records Golden Horde exchange through Saraychik toward Urgench and imported
objects from multiple regions. Our Sarai, Saraychik, Crimea and Central Asian
branches give this northern system a place in the map. They use approximate
anchors; the disputed identifications of individual Sarai sites are not resolved
by the coordinate. The Mongol states were separate and sometimes at war.

[Quanzhou’s Song–Yuan archaeology](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1561/)
supports its role as a major maritime hub. The view adds Chinese ceramics,
Quanzhou shipping and a Yuan capital connection, plus representative Venetian
and Genoese maritime links. These do not suggest that Rome still organized
all European commerce or that goods flowed in only the illustrated directions.
Coastal waypoints, portages and ocean legs remain schematic modern-geography
anchors. Each regional network requires more detail before use as a scholarly
route atlas.


## Sparse traffic experiment

Trade dots now arrive in irregular clusters with quiet gaps. This visual timing
is not calibrated to historical volumes. The cited evidence supports commodities,
connections and some individual cargoes, but does not provide a comparable
route-by-route and commodity-by-commodity series across all four periods.
Uluburun cargo composition must not be treated as an annual Mediterranean trade
ratio. Likewise [ORBIS](https://orbis.stanford.edu/orbis2012/ORBIS_v1paper_20120501.pdf)
models transport time/cost, not measured commodity throughput. All current routes
therefore use the same illustrative frequency distribution. Longer visible routes
can contain more dots because of their length, not higher historical volume.
No dot is a literal caravan, ship, coin, tonne or quantity of enslaved people.

Each route uses a stable random seed, independent gaps and clusters, and a long
animation cycle. These are presentation parameters only. Any future weighting
needs a cited, comparable measure with its period, units and uncertainty before
it can be encoded as frequency; price, cargo weight and caravan count are not
interchangeable.

## Wider Bronze Age and Roman-era additions (September 21)

- Indus–Gulf shipping: Harappan seals, carnelian beads and ivory at Ur and in the Gulf, and Mesopotamian texts naming Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus region), are summarized by [Britannica: Indus civilization](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Indus-civilization). The drawn lane from Lothal through Magan and Dilmun to Ur is schematic.
- Lapis lazuli: the Badakhshan mines of northeastern Afghanistan supplied Mesopotamia and Egypt throughout the Bronze Age ([Britannica: lapis lazuli](https://www.britannica.com/topic/lapis-lazuli)). The corridor through Balkh, Merv and the Iranian plateau is a reconstruction.
- Amber: Baltic amber reached Mycenaean shaft graves and, later, Rome by the Amber Road through Carnuntum and Aquileia ([Britannica: amber](https://www.britannica.com/science/amber)). The Bronze Age line is drawn fainter; the Roman-era road is well attested.
- Punt: Egyptian expeditions from the Red Sea port at Mersa Gawasis to Punt, probably on the southern Red Sea coast, brought incense, gold and ebony; the location of Punt is debated, so the line is uncertain ([Britannica: Punt](https://www.britannica.com/place/Punt)).
- Aksum and Adulis: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (already cited) describes Adulis as the port of the Aksumite kingdom trading ivory and other goods toward Roman Egypt.
